question: Your public API allows 100 requests per minute per key. Customers complain that a well-behaved integration gets 429s, while a badly written one still manages short floods. Which limiter fits best?
context: Clients are batch-oriented: they sync every few minutes and want to send a short burst, then go quiet. The limit exists to protect the database, which can absorb a brief spike but not a sustained one.

options.label: Fixed window counter per minute
options.why: Cheapest to build, but two clumps either side of a minute boundary are counted separately — so a client can push close to 200 requests in a few seconds while a client that syncs mid-window gets rejected.

options.label: Token bucket sized to the burst, refilling at the sustained rate
options.why: The bucket is exactly the "short burst is fine, sustained flood is not" policy: a client that has been quiet has a full bucket to spend, then settles to the refill rate. It is also O(1) state per key.

options.label: Sliding window log of every request timestamp
options.why: Precise and boundary-free, but it stores a timestamp per request per key and admits no deliberate burst. Correct behaviour, wrong shape for batch clients, and the most expensive option.

options.label: Leaky bucket that queues and drains at a fixed rate
options.why: Smooths the load on the database perfectly, but accepted requests wait in the queue — an API client sees latency instead of a clear 429, which is usually worse for an integration.
